sens: Man of the tribe of Judah, from the early period before the monarchy of Israel
H5900.detail: Iru is a man who lived in the tribe of Judah in ancient times, before the establishment of kingship in Israel. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:15, as the son of Caleb (the famous companion of Moses who explored Canaan) and the grandson of Jephunnah. His brothers were named Elah and Naam, and he himself had descendants.
H5900.origine: The name "Iru" literally means "watch" or "surveillance" in Hebrew, evoking the idea of someone who watches or observes. It is an ancient Hebrew name typical of the pre-monarchic period of Israel.
H5900.emploi: Iru is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in the genealogical record of 1 Chronicles 4:15. This passage lists the descendants of Caleb, one of the great figures of the Exodus and the conquest of Canaan. Iru appears in this list as a direct son of Caleb, testifying to the continuity of his tribal lineage.

sens: Son of Bela of the tribe of Benjamin
One of the family leaders of Benjamin during the time of Egypt and the desert
H5901.detail: Iri is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Bela. He is presented in 1 Chronicles 7:7 as one of the five sons of Bela, all recognized as leaders of their father's houses and valiant men. His name appears in the genealogy of the Benjamites and in the census that recorded twenty-two thousand thirty-four warriors from this lineage.
H5901.origine: The name Iri means "belonging to a city" in Hebrew, formed from the root referring to the city. It expresses the idea of one who is connected to a city, perhaps as an inhabitant or as a founder.
H5901.emploi: Iri appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:7, in the genealogy of the sons of Bela. He is counted among the descendants of Benjamin and recognized as a family leader during the time of Egypt and the desert. His name is recorded alongside his brothers Etsbon, Uzzi, Uziel, and Jeremoth, all distinguished for their valor and family authority.

sens: Edomite chief during the Patriarchs' era
H5902.detail: Iram is one of the Edomite chiefs mentioned in the genealogy of Esau. He appears in the list of Edomite chiefs, alongside Magdiel and others (Genesis 36:43 and 1 Chronicles 1:54). His name suggests a connection to a city or an urban establishment.
H5902.origine: The name means "belonging to a city." He is an Edomite chief whose name likely reflects his role as a governor attached to an important region or settlement.
H5902.emploi: Iram appears twice in the Bible, always in genealogical lists: in Genesis 36:43, where he is presented as one of the chiefs of Edom according to their dwellings, and in 1 Chronicles 1:54, where the same list is repeated. These two references constitute the entirety of his biblical mentions. He is among the descendants of Esau, with no personal narrative attached to his name.

sens: without clothing
devoid of protection or resources
exposed to view, uncovered
H5903.detail:
1. Nu means to be without clothing, the body fully uncovered. This is the literal sense: after eating the forbidden fruit, Adam and Eve "knew that they were naked" (Genesis 3:7) and suddenly became aware of their nakedness.

2. The word also denotes a state of complete destitution, total lack of resources or protection. In the threats of Deuteronomy, the one who disobeys will serve "in hunger, thirst, nakedness, and lack" (Deuteronomy 28:48) — nakedness here represents misery, the absence of clothing to cover and protect oneself.

3. Nu can mean exposed or defenseless: the city of Jerusalem, in Ezekiel's vision, was "naked," vulnerable and unprotected, "bathed in its blood" (Ezekiel 16:22), an image of its abandonment and fragile state.
H5903.origine: The Hebrew word עֵירֹם comes from a root that expresses the idea of being stripped bare, of exposure. It belongs to the family of verbs and nouns related to undressing or exposure. This word also has a close relationship with the idea of shameful or vulnerable nakedness, often linked in the Old Testament to humiliation or total destitution.
H5903.emploi: This word appears ten times in the Old Testament, mainly in the accounts of Ezekiel and at the beginning of Genesis. It is first used in the literal and concrete sense: the nakedness of Adam and Eve after sin, expressing their sudden guilt and vulnerability (Genesis 3:7-11). It also denotes nakedness as misfortune or dishonor: in the prophets, being naked symbolizes the miserable state of a people stripped of their goods, delivered to their enemies, reduced to slavery (Ezekiel 16:7, 16:22; Deuteronomy 28:48). It is a serious word, laden with shame and distress in most of its biblical uses.
H5903.portee: For the reader, this word reveals that nakedness in the Bible is never neutral: it speaks of sin, of man's vulnerability before God and judgment. It also reminds us that the lack of clothing symbolizes total destitution, loss of dignity and protection. That is why covering, clothing, represents in the Bible grace, divine protection, and the restoration of man — a theme that culminates in the robe of righteousness granted by God.

sens: City of the tribe of Dan in Canaan
H5905.detail: Ir-Schémesch is a city of the tribe of Dan, mentioned only once in the Bible as part of the territory assigned to this tribe during the division of Canaan (Joshua 19:41). Its name literally means "city of the sun" in Hebrew (ir = city, shémesh = sun), probably referring to a sanctuary or a solar deity that was worshiped there before the Israelite conquest. It is likely the same place as Beth-Shemesh, another important city in the territory of Dan and Judah.
H5905.origine: The Hebrew name עִיר שָׁמֶשׁ is composed of two elements: עִיר (ir, "city") and שָׁמֶשׁ (shémesh, "sun"). The word shémesh denotes the sun in the Old Testament and evokes the solar deities of the ancient Near East. This same place name appears in the form Beth-Shemesh ("house of the sun") in several biblical passages, suggesting that these two names likely refer to the same location or variants of the same toponym.
H5905.emploi: Ir-Schémesch appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:41, in the list of cities assigned to the tribe of Dan during the division of Canaan after the conquest. It is listed among the border cities of the Danite territory, alongside Zorea and Eshtaol. This unique mention suggests that it may have been a secondary locality or that it was better known by its other name, Beth-Shemesh.

sens: Constellation of stars visible in the northern night sky
The Great Bear, also called the Plough
H5906.detail:
1. The Bear is a constellation — a grouping of stars — that the ancients saw as resembling a bear in the night sky. It is one of the most visible and recognizable constellations in the Northern Hemisphere. Job 9:9 mentions it alongside Orion and the Pleiades, indicating it is among the greatest and most beautiful celestial bodies.
2. The Great Bear served as a guide for navigation and orientation, particularly because it points towards the North Star. In Job 38:32, God asks Job if he can "lead the Great Bear with its cubs," which evokes its regular and predictable movement around the celestial pole: it is an image of order and mastery of the cosmos.
H5906.origine: The Hebrew word עַיִשׁ (ayish) comes from a root that means "bear" (land animal), because the ancient Hebrews and other peoples saw in this grouping of stars the silhouette of a bear. In Greek, the same constellation is called Arktos, a word that also means "bear": all ancient peoples made this same visual connection. The name "Great Bear" was commonly used to designate the brightest and most visible constellation in this family of stars.
H5906.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the book of Job, in passages where God questions Job about his knowledge of the cosmos. In Job 9:9, it is included in a list of celestial wonders created by God. In Job 38:32, it becomes an example of those cosmic realities that only God can govern and orient in the sky. These two contexts emphasize that the Bear is not merely an ornament of the sky, but a testimony to divine order and wisdom.
H5906.portee: The Great Bear reminds the reader that God created and orders the entire universe according to His wisdom. For ancient biblical readers, recognizing this constellation in the sky was an invitation to meditate on God's creative power and the impossibility for man to master or fully understand the cosmos without Him — a central theme in God's discourse in Job.

sens: Father of King Baal-Hanan of Edom
Character from the patriarchal era
Name meaning "mouse" in Hebrew
H5907G.detail: 1. Acbor is the father of King Baal-Hanan, who reigned over Edom after the death of King Saul. His name appears in the genealogy of the kings of Edom, where it states that "Baal-Hanan, son of Acbor, reigned in his place" when Saul died (Genesis 36:38). 2. Acbor lived during the patriarchal era, as confirmed by his mention in ancient genealogical lists. He represents a figure in the history of Edom, one of Israel's neighboring nations. 3. The name "Acbor" literally means "mouse" in Hebrew, which was a common name for a person at the time, with no particular link to the animal.
H5907G.origine: The Hebrew name עַכְבּוֹר (akhbor) derives from a root that means "mouse." It was a common human name in the ancient Semitic world, where animals often served as the basis for proper names. The name does not reflect a particular characteristic of Acbor, but simply the onomastic taste of his time.
H5907G.emploi: Acbor appears only three times in the Bible, all in the genealogy of the kings of Edom. In Genesis 36:38-39, he is mentioned as the father of King Baal-Hanan; the text simply indicates that this king succeeded Saul of Edom and that he himself was succeeded by King Hadar. The same information appears in the genealogical summary of 1 Chronicles 1:49. Acbor is thus a minor figure, known only because he was the father of an Edomite king, and no details of his life are given.

sens: High official in the kingdom of Judah under King Josiah
H5907H.detail: Acbor is a high-ranking figure in the administration of the kingdom of Judah, living during the time of King Josiah (around the 7th century BC). He is sent on an official mission to the prophetess Huldah to ask for the interpretation of the Law discovered in the Temple (2 Kings 22:12-14). His son Elnathan becomes an influential man at court, particularly during the reading of the scroll of Jeremiah before the leaders of the kingdom (Jeremiah 36:12).
H5907H.origine: The name Acbor means "mouse" in Hebrew. It is a common personal name in ancient Israel, although it has an animal connotation. The same man is also called Abdon in the second book of Chronicles (34:20), showing that alternative names existed in biblical tradition.
H5907H.emploi: Acbor appears four times in the Old Testament, always in the political and religious context of Judah in the 7th century. First, he is mentioned as one of the high officials sent by King Josiah to consult the prophetess Huldah about the book of the Law discovered in the Temple (2 Kings 22:12, 22:14). Then, his son Elnathan plays an active role during the crisis caused by Jeremiah's preaching and the reading of his scroll before the princes (Jeremiah 26:22 and 36:12), which shows that Acbor's family maintained considerable influence in the circles of Judean power.
H5907H.portee: Acbor represents an example of a royal high official who, at a crucial moment for Judah, intervenes in discerning God's will through the prophetess. His involvement in King Josiah's religious reform and his engagement in prophetic affairs demonstrate that in Israel, even the powerful of this world needed to seek the word of the Lord.

sens: Small animal that weaves webs to catch insects
Delicate and fine web woven by the spider
Image of fragility, instability, of what cannot support
H5908.detail:
1. The spider is a small animal known for its ability to weave a web: it is a delicate trap that it constructs to catch its prey. The Hebrew word refers to the animal itself.
2. The spider's web is the fine and light network that the spider weaves: Job 8:14 specifically mentions "spider's web" to describe something that cannot support, that collapses.
3. In the Bible, the spider and its web become a powerful image of what is fragile and without foundation: it symbolizes instability and futility. In Isaiah 59:5, those who "weave spider's webs" commit evil and vain acts, completely incapable of protecting or saving.
H5908.origine: The Hebrew word is an onomatopoeia evoking the rapid weaving and buzzing of the animal. It is rare in the Bible and does not seem to have other notable derived forms. The image of the spider and its fragility was already known in the ancient Near East.
H5908.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Old Testament, and in both cases to describe fragility and instability. In Job 8:14, Job says that the one who rejects God has for support a "spider's web": his assurance collapses like this delicate web. In Isaiah 59:5, the wicked "weave spider's webs," an image of their evil works that are vain and without strength. The Bible thus uses this small animal to express the idea of futility and fragility in the face of God's power.
H5908.portee: The spider reminds the believer that everything not founded on God is frail and cannot endure. It invites one not to place trust in vain things or human pride: these things collapse like a web. It is an invitation to seek a solid and lasting foundation, not in our own strength, but in the stability that only God can provide.

sens: Small rodent that ravages crops and homes
Gold representation or statue of this animal
Plague or scourge sent by God
H5909.detail:
1. The mouse is a small animal that crawls on the ground and is a rodent. It is classified among the unclean animals according to the law of Moses (Leviticus 11:29), which means it was not to be eaten. In the daily life of the people of Israel, mice caused significant damage, particularly to crops and provisions.
2. The Philistines, struck by a plague of mice that ravaged their land, made figures or statuettes of mice in gold to offer to the Lord as a sign of repentance (1 Samuel 6:4-5, 6:11, 6:18). These gold representations accompanied the holy ark they were returning to Israel. Each Philistine leader sent a golden mouse, one for each city.
3. In the prophetic context of Isaiah 66:17, eating a mouse, like eating pork, is an act of impurity and rebellion against God, leading to the destruction of the one who commits it. The mouse here represents what defiles and opposes the holiness of the Lord.
H5909.origine: The Hebrew word עַכְבָּר (akhbar) refers to the small rodent known since antiquity in the Near East. Its exact etymology is not firmly established, but the word appears in other Semitic languages with a similar meaning. In Aramaic, for example, similar forms can be found. The word refers to a real animal, one that lives near human dwellings and causes destruction.
H5909.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, always in singular or plural without variation in meaning. It primarily designates the real animal, forbidden for consumption according to the Mosaic law (Leviticus 11:29). Then, it takes on a more specific meaning in the story of the Philistines and the ark: it refers to the golden figurines that they made and offered to Israel in recognition of the plague that struck them (1 Samuel 6). Finally, in Isaiah, it symbolizes ritual impurity and unfaithfulness to the covenant: eating a mouse is an act that provokes God's anger and condemnation.
H5909.portee: The mouse reminds the believer that the law of Moses established precise distinctions between the clean and the unclean, between what honors God and what dishonors Him. The story of the Philistines teaches that even Israel's enemies are compelled to recognize the power of the Lord. Isaiah shows that rejecting divine ordinances, even in small details, leads to God's judgment.

sens: Maritime port in Phoenicia, coastal city of the territory of Asher
H5910.detail: Acco was an important port city on the Levantine coast, located north of Mount Carmel and south of Tyre, in the region assigned to the tribe of Asher. It was inhabited by Canaanites who were not driven out despite Israel's conquest (Judges 1:31). This city was also known by the Greek name Ptolemais.
H5910.origine: The name "Acco" literally means "its distress" or "its discomfort" in Hebrew, perhaps referring to the difficulties of the site or the confined nature of the port. It is an ancient Phoenician port, one of the oldest cities in the region.
H5910.emploi: Acco appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Judges 1:31, where it is mentioned among the Canaanite cities that the tribe of Asher could not conquer. It is a concrete example of the incompleteness of Israel's conquest: the original inhabitants remained. Historically, this city became a major port and was known in Greek as Ptolemais in later periods.
H5910.portee: This verse reminds us of a human reality in biblical life: the promised victory was never complete without the obedience of the people. Acco symbolizes the compromises with paganism that characterized this era, inviting the reader to reflect on the obstacles that Israel had to overcome.

sens: Valley of Judah where Achan was executed
Site of a historical tragedy
Symbol of trouble and divine judgment
Sign of future hope
H5911.detail: 1. Achor is a valley located in Judah, between Jericho and Debir. Its name literally means "trouble" or "disturbance" in Hebrew, which recalls the grave incident that took place there: after the fall of Jericho, the warrior Achan stole from the devoted spoils to God, bringing disaster upon all Israel (Joshua 7:24-26). 2. The valley is the site where Achan and his family were stoned in divine judgment for this sacrilegious theft, giving rise to the name that persists to the days of Joshua (Joshua 7:26). It is a place marked by the necessity of judgment and purification of the community of Israel. 3. In the Old Testament, the valley of Achor symbolizes the consequence of sin and the terrible intervention of God against the one who troubles the faithfulness of the chosen people. 4. Paradoxically, Isaiah and Hosea announce a future restoration where this valley of trouble becomes a sign of hope and blessing for the repentant people (Isaiah 65:10; Hosea 2:17), showing the divine mercy that transforms even places of judgment into promises of salvation.
H5911.origine: The Hebrew name עָכוֹר (akhor) comes from a root meaning "to trouble" or "to disturb." The valley takes its name from the dramatic event in Joshua 7, where Achan caused trouble (in Hebrew, the word also applies to Achan himself, called "Achan son of Zerah, the one who caused trouble in Israel"). The name remains in the geography of Israel as a perpetual reminder of this incident: not only of the executed judgment but also of the moral lesson it teaches the people.
H5911.emploi: The valley of Achor appears five times in the Old Testament, first as a geographical landmark in the description of the borders of Judah (Joshua 15:7). Its first historical role is the site of the execution of Achan and his family after the theft of devoted spoils (Joshua 7:24, 7:26). Later, the prophets Isaiah and Hosea invoke this valley differently: no longer as a place of curse, but as a symbol of transformation and restoration. Isaiah sees the flock grazing peacefully in the valley of Achor (Isaiah 65:10), while Hosea announces that God will give vineyards to restored Israel, making the valley of trouble a "door of hope" (Hosea 2:17). This transition from judgment to hope reflects the entire arc of salvation history: from condemnation to redemption.
H5911.portee: For the Christian reader, the valley of Achor reminds us that sin has concrete consequences and that God takes seriously the violation of His covenant; however, it also testifies that even in the places most marked by judgment, God can restore and make hope flourish. It is an invitation to repentance and trust in divine mercy.

sens: A man from the tribe of Judah during the conquest of Canaan
The one who violated the ban by keeping for himself some of the spoils from Jericho
A symbol of sin that troubles the entire people
H5912.detail:
1. Achan was a man from the tribe of Judah, living at the time when Israel was entering Canaan under the leadership of Joshua. His name means "trouble" in Hebrew, which foreshadows his disastrous role in history.

2. While God had commanded that all the spoils of Jericho be destroyed or given to the Lord's treasury, Achan secretly kept for himself a valuable cloak, silver, and a bar of gold (Joshua 7:20-21). This theft of items that had been devoted to the ban was a serious act of rebellion.

3. His sin had terrible consequences: Israel suffered a humiliating defeat at Ai, and then the entire assembly discovered him and had him stoned to death, along with his entire family (Joshua 7:24). The text shows that his crime brought weakness to the whole people, hence the importance given to his judgment.
H5912.origine: The name literally means "to trouble" or "to cause trouble." It is a proper name that carries meaning: it reveals Achan's role as one who brings disorder and defeat to Israel through his disobedience. In biblical history, the sin of one can affect the entire community.
H5912.emploi: Achan appears six times in the Bible, all in the book of Joshua, chapters 7 and 22. His story occupies the entirety of chapter 7: after the miraculous capture of Jericho, Achan is identified by lot (Joshua 7:18), confesses his crime (Joshua 7:19-20), and perishes with his family (Joshua 7:24). Joshua 22:20 mentions him again as an example of a serious crime that provoked God's anger against all Israel. His case illustrates the importance of obedience to God's specific commandments, especially regarding consecrated things.
H5912.portee: The story of Achan teaches the believer that hidden sin affects the community, and that obedience to God in small matters is not a detail. It also shows that even after great miracles (the fall of Jericho), the temptation of covetousness remains present. Achan's judgment finally reveals God's holiness: He does not tolerate the violation of His bans, even though He always offers the possibility to confess one's sin.

sens: To produce a sound of ringing or clinking
H5913.detail: 1. The verb literally means to make noise by ringing or clinking something — here the bracelets and anklets that women wore on their ankles and feet. It is a light and repetitive sound, the kind produced by metal when it strikes. In Isaiah 3:16, the daughters of Zion are criticized for intentionally making these ornaments resound by walking with affected small steps, which was a sign of vanity and pride: they sought to draw attention to their beauty and wealth.
H5913.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of producing a metallic sound or making noise. It is formed to imitate the actual sound made by metallic objects when they strike — it is an imitative word, created to evoke the noise itself. The form used here (Piel) intensifies the action: it is not an accidental sound, but a deliberately repeated and emphasized action.
H5913.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 3:16. There, God describes the behavior of the wealthy women of Jerusalem at the time of the prophet: they wore precious ornaments (chains, bracelets, anklets) and walked in an affected manner so that everyone could hear the noise they made. It was an outward sign of their vanity, their desire to show off, and display their wealth. The context clearly shows that this behavior is presented as reprehensible: it is pride that God judges.
H5913.portee: This word illustrates how the Bible judges pride, not only in the intentions of the heart but in gestures and habits. Intentionally making noise to draw attention to oneself is a subtle yet real form of vanity. The text invites the reader to examine their own behaviors: do we seek to show off, to impress, to be noticed? True beauty, according to Scripture, comes from a gentle and quiet spirit, not from the need to parade.

sens: Metal ornament worn by women around the ankle
Link or shackle that holds someone back
H5914.detail:
1. An anklet or bracelet made of metal (gold, silver, bronze) that women attach to their ankle as adornment: in Isaiah 3:18, the Lord denounces the pride of the women of Jerusalem who adorn themselves with "anklets" on their "feet," luxury jewelry that manifests their vanity.
2. By extension, a chain that imprisons or restrains: in Proverbs 7:22, the duped young man follows the adulterous woman "like an ox going to the slaughter," "bound" by the illusion of pleasure — the word evokes both the shiny bracelet that fascinates the eye and the invisible bonds of seduction that enslave the heart.
H5914.origine: The Hebrew word ekhs primarily refers to the anklet, a typical personal ornament for women in the ancient Near East. The root conveys the idea of surrounding or encircling, which corresponds well to the function of the anklet that encircles the ankle. The image of the link naturally follows: what adorns can also chain.
H5914.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Isaiah 3:18, it is part of the list of luxurious female jewelry that God will remove in judgment; here it is a simple ornament. In Proverbs 7:22, it takes on a metaphorical value: the young man is "bound" like by invisible chains by the allure of the adulterous woman, suggesting that his heart has been chained by the illusion of pleasure. Both uses show the transition from the concrete (the jewelry) to the figurative (moral captivity).
H5914.portee: For the Christian, this word invites meditation on the seduction of luxury and the slavery of sin. The anklet that adorns and fascinates can become the chain that imprisons: the shine of what seduces the senses often hides a hidden servitude. Proverbs 7 warns men not to be seduced by what shines, for it is a path to moral death.

sens: A woman from the time of the Judges, daughter of Caleb
Wife of Othniel, her father's nephew
H5915G.detail:
1. Achsa is the daughter of Caleb, the valiant warrior and scout who conquered Hebron. Her father promises her in marriage to whoever can conquer the city of Kirjath-sepher (Joshua 15:16; Judges 1:12). This is a prize reserved for the bravest, a mark of honor in ancient Israel.

2. Othniel, son of Kenaz and Caleb's younger brother, wins this challenge: he captures the city and receives Achsa as his wife (Joshua 15:17; Judges 1:13). Thus, she becomes the wife of the future judge of Israel, linked to her family through this courageous marriage. The biblical text tells us nothing else about her personal life, but her name and story remain etched in Israel's memory.
H5915G.origine: The name means "anklet" or "ankle ring" — an ornament worn on the ankles, symbolizing beauty and grace. It is a poetic and refined name, typical of ancient Hebrew onomastics, which reveals the character or appearance of a person. The name expresses elegance and perhaps the dignity of this woman of high lineage.
H5915G.emploi: Achsa appears only four times in the Bible, twice in the book of Joshua (15:16 and 15:17) and twice in the book of Judges (1:12 and 1:13) — the same events recounted in duplicate. She is always in the context of Caleb's promise and her marriage to Othniel. Her role is limited but memorable: she is the prize and reward for military courage, reflecting the importance of marriage and lineage in Israelite life during the time of conquest and the Judges. No particular action is attributed to her, but her presence underscores the family alliance sealed by this strategic and honorable marriage.

sens: Daughter of Caleb
Wife of Othniel
H5915H.detail: Acsa is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:49, where she is identified as the daughter of Caleb. Her name means "anklet" or "ankle ring" in Hebrew, an image evoking delicacy and elegance. According to the parallel accounts in the Book of Judges, Caleb gave her in marriage to his brother Othniel as a reward for conquering the city of Debir, making her a woman of the tribe of Judah at the time of the Exodus and the wilderness.
H5915H.origine: The name Acsa comes from the Hebrew עַכְסָה (akhsah), whose etymology suggests the image of a chain or ring worn at the ankle — a delicate adornment. Although this name appears only once in this genealogical passage, it bears witness to how Scripture preserves the names of important women in the history of Israel, including those from the lineage of Caleb.
H5915H.emploi: Acsa is mentioned only once in 1 Chronicles 2:49, in a genealogical list that enumerates the children of Caleb. She is simply referred to as "the daughter of Caleb." However, the Book of Judges (1:12-15 and 3:11) tells us more about her: she was given in marriage to Othniel, who had won the victory over Debir, and she even interceded with her father for springs of water in Canaan. These passages show that she was a woman of initiative and courage, not passive in the history of Israel.
H5915H.portee: Acsa reminds us that God sees and honors courageous women. Her story, though briefly mentioned here, reveals a woman who actively participated in establishing Israel in Canaan — first by agreeing to marry Othniel to reward his military victory, and then by boldly interceding for her family's interests. She embodies the quiet strength of women of faith in God's purpose.

sens: To disturb someone, to put them in difficulty or danger
To agitate, to disorder a situation or a community
To cause misfortune or calamity
To be disturbed, agitated, or troubled (passive form)
H5916.detail:
1. To disturb someone directly, to put them in embarrassment or expose them to danger: Jacob says to his sons, "You are troubling me, by making me odious to the inhabitants of the land" (Genesis 34:30), for their action makes him suspicious in the eyes of his neighbors.
2. To agitate an entire community, to create public disorder or tumult: Elijah asserts, "I do not trouble Israel" (1 Kings 18:18), refuting the accusation that his actions cause chaos in the kingdom.
3. To cause misfortune or ruin, particularly in a household or family: "He who troubles his house will inherit the wind" (Proverbs 11:29) means that he who sows disorder in his home will reap emptiness and loss.
4. To be oneself troubled, agitated, or afflicted (when reading the text in the passive sense): "my pain was no less intense" (Psalms 39:3) expresses the inner turmoil of one who suffers in silence.
H5916.origine: The Hebrew verb עָכַר (achar) literally means "to agitate" or "to trouble." The root evokes the idea of stirring up, disordering what was calm or orderly. This family of words appears in other passages where trouble affects individuals or entire situations, each time associated with a disturbance that creates discomfort or danger.
H5916.emploi: This verb appears 13 times primarily in biblical narratives and wisdom literature. In the historical Old Testament, it describes human actions that create disorder: Jacob is troubled by his sons (Genesis 34:30), Joshua accuses Achan of troubling Israel (Joshua 7:25). In the wisdom books, especially Proverbs, it characterizes one who troubles his own house and suffers the consequences (Proverbs 11:29). The word always carries a negative nuance: the one who troubles is responsible for the ensuing misfortune, whether it affects his family, his community, or his own heart.
H5916.portee: This word reminds the reader that there are consequences to our actions: to trouble others is to reap trouble. It invites us to examine whether our words or actions cause disorder around us, and it highlights each person's responsibility for the peace of their home and community. It is a call to wisdom and restraint.

sens: A man of the tribe of Judah
He who violated the divine ban at Jericho
Symbol of transgression and its consequences
H5917.detail: Acar is a man of the tribe of Judah, son of Carmi, who lived at the time of the conquest of Canaan before the establishment of the Israelite monarchy. He is best known for violating God's formal order prohibiting the taking of spoils from the city of Jericho: despite this prohibition, he secretly kept part of the spoils, which provoked God's anger against all Israel and caused the defeat at Ai. Discovered, he was sentenced to death and executed by stoning, along with his entire family, to atone for this infidelity to the Lord. His name means "to trouble," and that is exactly what he did: he troubled Israel through his disobedience (1 Chronicles 2:7).
H5917.origine: The name Acar literally means "to trouble" or "to cause trouble." This meaning is not accidental: it summarizes God's judgment on this man whose transgression brought disorder and misfortune to the entire community of Israel. Another form of the same name, Achan, exists in biblical texts and refers to the same person. The etymology of the name reflects the action that made him memorable.
H5917.emploi: Acar appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:7, where he is listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah as the son of Carmi. This text qualifies him as the one "who troubled Israel when he committed an infidelity regarding the devoted things." Although mentioned only once by this name in Chronicles, his complete story is told in detail in the book of Joshua (chapters 7 and 8), where he is called Achan. His account illustrates the importance of total obedience to God and the serious consequences of transgression, even individual, which reverberates throughout the community.
H5917.portee: The story of Acar teaches the Christian reader a decisive spiritual truth: hidden disobedience to God, even in an apparently insignificant detail, has repercussions that go far beyond the sinner himself and affect the entire community. It reminds us that integrity and honesty in obedience are essential, and that no secret remains hidden before the Lord. It is also a warning against covetousness that leads astray and causes downfall.

sens: Father of Paguiel
Tribe leader at the time of the Exodus
H5918.detail: Ocran is a man who lived during the time of the Exodus and the wilderness. He is the father of Paguiel, who becomes the prince (leader) of the tribe of Asher and is among the twelve princes chosen to lead the tribes of Israel (Numbers 1:13). His name means "he who troubles" or "disturber," an image that evokes instability or disorder. Ocran himself does not act in the biblical narrative: he is primarily known as the father of this important tribe leader. He is mentioned five times in the book of Numbers, each time to identify Paguiel as "son of Ocran" (Numbers 2:27; 7:72; 10:26).
H5918.origine: The name Ocran comes from the Hebrew root עכר (akhar), which means "to trouble" or "to disturb." This same root appears in the story of Achan (Joshua 7), whose name comes from the same verb and who "troubles" Israel through his disobedience. The suffix -an forms a proper name. In Hebrew, this type of name often expresses a character trait or a significant event related to the person.
H5918.emploi: Ocran is mentioned only in the book of Numbers, always as the father of the prince Paguiel. He first appears in the census of the tribes at Sinai (Numbers 1:13), where Paguiel is designated as the prince of Asher. He is then cited in the order of march of the camp (Numbers 2:27), during the offerings of the princes at the Tabernacle, where Paguiel son of Ocran brings his sacrifice (Numbers 7:72-77), and finally in the order of march toward Canaan (Numbers 10:26). Ocran never intervenes directly: he is the father who confers his genealogical identity to an important tribe leader.

sens: Venomous snake with deadly venom
Figure of malice and deadly words
H5919.detail:
1. The asp is a small venomous snake, very dangerous for its size. In Psalm 140:4, the poet mentions it to speak of the deadly venom it produces — an image of the danger it carries within.
2. The Bible often uses venomous snakes as symbols of human malice. When the psalmist says that his enemies "have venom of asps under their lips," he is not talking about real snakes, but about poisoned words, hurtful, deadly to those who endure them — slanders, threats, insults that wound like venom.
H5919.origine: The Hebrew word akh.shuv refers to a small venomous snake, probably the asp, a snake known in the Mediterranean and ancient Near East. The image of the snake, with its venom and sneaky movements, has always struck the biblical imagination as a symbol of what destroys stealthily and without warning.
H5919.emploi: The word appears only once in Hebrew in the Bible, in Psalm 140:4. It fits into a long biblical tradition where venomous snakes represent malicious speech and hidden malice. The context is a prayer of an oppressed person asking God to protect him from those who persecute him and whose words deeply wound him.
H5919.portee: This word shows us how seriously the Bible takes the destructive power of human speech — it can kill as surely as venom. The believer reading this psalm learns to recognize within himself the temptation of poisoned words, and to pray that God keeps him from a tongue that kills. It is a call to moral vigilance over our words.

sens: That which is above, rising vertically
That which ascends toward heaven or toward God
Dignity, moral or social elevation
Exaltation, greatness
H5920H.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes physical height, that which is above the ground or rises in the air — like a mountain or the top of a building. This is the primary image: the space upward, verticality. 2. It then applies to the space that ascends toward heaven, where God dwells. When one cries "on high" (Psalm 50:4), one addresses their voice toward God who is above. 3. The word acquires a moral and social sense: it describes a prominent place, dignity, honor. David is "the high man" (2 Samuel 23:1), not because he is physically tall, but because he occupies a position of authority and glory. 4. In some contexts, it expresses exaltation, spiritual elevation, or prestige — the greatness of a person or work.
H5920H.origine: The Hebrew word עַל comes from a root expressing the idea of ascending, rising up. The same root appears in other Hebrew words related to height and altitude. The fundamental image is that of upward movement, surpassing the ground level. This root is also found in biblical contexts where God is described as the Most High, who dwells "on high" — that is, beyond, above creation.
H5920H.emploi: This word appears four times in the noted usages, especially in biblical poetry and in the psalms. In 2 Samuel 23:1, it qualifies David as "the high man," emphasizing his royal status and dignity. In Psalm 50:4, the expression "crying on high" refers to the call directed toward heaven, toward God who sits above. The word thus navigates between the concrete sense (height, superior space) and the figurative sense (honor, dignity, call to the divine). It also appears in Hosea, where contexts seem to play on this tension between physical and moral elevation.
H5920H.portee: Understanding this word helps to grasp how the Bible speaks of God: He is "high," inaccessible and transcendent, remaining above His creation. But it also describes human beings who receive honor and authority: they are "elevated," placed in a position of responsibility and glory. This language of height expresses both respect for what surpasses and the call to direct our gaze and hearts toward what is above — toward God.

sens: Position above a surface or being
Movement toward a person or place
Domain or subject of discussion
Basis, reason, or justification
Responsibility or charge entrusted to someone
Opposition or hostility
H5921A.detail:
1. The most common and concrete meaning: something placed, situated, or positioned above a surface. Examples: the Spirit of God moved upon the waters (Genesis 1:2), or the ark of the covenant appears upon the cloud (Genesis 9:14).

2. The movement of a person toward another, an attack or invasion launched against a territory. Examples: when an invasion is made upon the territory of Judah (1 Samuel 30:14), or when the flood comes upon the earth (Genesis 6:17).

3. The object or subject being discussed, what concerns someone or something. Example: when the Lord speaks upon you, Baruch (Jeremiah 45:2).

4. The reason, motive, or foundation of an action. One acts "upon" a given basis, "according to" or "by virtue of" something.

5. The responsibility placed upon someone, a charge or task that falls to them. Example: the Levites carry the tabernacle (Numbers 1:50).

6. Opposition, hostility, or conflict: acting against someone or something.
H5921A.origine: This preposition is very common in biblical Hebrew. It comes from the image of "lifting" or "going over." It is found in many compound expressions that modify its meaning: it can indicate position, movement, causality, or dominion. It is one of the most flexible and frequently used prepositions, as it adapts to context to express spatial, temporal, logical, or relational relationships.
H5921A.emploi: This preposition is among the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible (4482 usages). It appears in all books, from the Pentateuch to the Prophets and the Writings. It primarily marks spatial relationships: "upon the earth," "upon the waters." It then expresses movement or action directed toward a goal or against a target: invading a territory, walking toward someone. It also serves to introduce a reason or basis: acting according to a motive. Finally, it can designate the responsibility or charge entrusted to someone. Its meaning varies considerably depending on the verb or context: with a verb of movement, it indicates direction; with a verb of action, often opposition; with a noun, position or subject.
H5921A.portee: This small, omnipresent preposition reminds us that every human action is situated "under" something: an intention, a reason, an order, or the hand of God. Understanding its nuances helps to grasp how the Bible expresses both submission to God (living "under" His law and grace) and spiritual warfare (acting "against" evil). It invites reflection on what "justifies" or "grounds" our actions.

sens: Introduces the cause or reason for an action
Marks a reason that justifies or explains what precedes
Expresses a condition or circumstance
Can introduce a concession or an objection
H5921B.detail:
1. The word introduces the direct cause of an action: Abraham says to his guests, "I will take a piece of bread, for that is why you have passed by your servant" (Genesis 18:5) — he explains why he wants to feed them. This answers the question "why?"
2. It marks the reason that justifies a previous word or decision: Jacob refuses his brother's gift, "for that is why I have looked at your face as one looks at the face of God" (Genesis 33:10) — he gives the reason why the gift is sufficient for him.
3. It can express a condition or circumstance that makes an action impossible or necessary: "Because you have turned away from the Lord, the Lord will not be with you" (Numbers 14:43) — the action of the Israelites justifies God's absence.
4. Rarely, it introduces a slight concession or objection: "Do nothing to these men since they have come under the shadow of my roof" (Genesis 19:8) — the presence under the roof is a reason to spare them.
H5921B.origine: This conjunction combines two Hebrew words: "כִּי" (ki, "that") and "עַל כֵּן" (al ken, literally "upon thus", meaning "for this reason"). Together, they form a powerful causal conjunction that links an action to its cause. The structure "כִּי עַל כֵּן" emphasizes the logical and causal sequence of events: first the reason, then the consequence.
H5921B.emploi: This conjunction appears ten times in the provided passages, mainly in the narratives of Genesis and the beginning of Exodus, as well as in the prophetic words of Jeremiah. It is one of the most common tools for linking cause and effect in the biblical narrative. It is also found in situations where someone must justify their decision or action before an interlocutor. In Numbers 14:43, it intervenes in a divine warning: Moses explains why defeat is inevitable. In 2 Samuel 18:20 and Jeremiah 38:4, it expresses an argument or reason opposing a contemplated action. It is flexible: it can introduce an immediate cause, a deeper reason, or even a delicate objection.
H5921B.portee: For the Christian reader, this conjunction reveals how the Bible links actions to their consequences. It shows that nothing happens by chance: every action has a reason, every event a cause. This is important for understanding God's justice and human responsibility. When Abraham feeds his guests "for" it is his duty of hospitality, or when the Lord does not save a rebellious people "because" they have turned away from Him, we see that God acts with logic and fairness. This word invites us to seek the deeper reasons behind biblical events and to recognize that our choices have consequences.

sens: On the surface of, in contact with something
Above, dominating or extending beyond
About, concerning, regarding
Towards, against
Near, close to, in the presence of
H5922.detail:
1. On the surface of, in contact with: the simplest and most concrete meaning. Daniel sees a vision "on" his bed (Daniel 4:10), meaning he is lying down and the vision manifests while he is reclining.
2. Above, dominating: indicates a position of superiority or an extension beyond. When the king speaks of something "on" a subject, he reigns over that matter, he has authority (Daniel 6:1 refers to the king and his governors).
3. About, concerning: introduces the theme being discussed. The letter is written "concerning" Jerusalem (Ezra 4:8), and the king asks for a decision "on" this matter (Ezra 5:17) — the word designates what the communication is about.
4. Towards, against: expresses movement or opposition. Rehum and Shimshai write "against" Jerusalem implicitly, accusing (Ezra 4:8-12), which opposes the reconstruction.
5. Near, close to: indicates personal proximity. Daniel goes "to" Arioch (Daniel 2:24) to address him directly.
H5922.origine: This preposition comes from a Semitic root expressing the idea of "rising above" and "being on." It is one of the oldest and most universal in Semitic languages. It appears throughout the Hebrew and Aramaic Old Testament with great flexibility of meaning: depending on the context, it can mean "on", "about", "against", "towards". In Greek, it often corresponds to ἐπί (epi), which shares the same versatility.
H5922.emploi: This word is one of the most frequent prepositions in the Old Testament. In the provided usages (Ezra and Daniel), it appears 86 times. It primarily expresses physical position: being "on" his bed, being "restored" (put back) in his kingdom. Very often, it introduces the subject or theme of an action: writing "concerning" Jerusalem, asking for a decision "on" the construction of the temple, speaking "about" a royal defense. It can also mark direction or opposition: being "against" something. Finally, it sometimes expresses proximity: coming "to" someone. Its meaning varies slightly depending on the verb it accompanies, which shows the flexibility of this preposition in biblical Aramaic.
H5922.portee: This ordinary preposition conveys a lesson for the believer: it shows how the Bible unfolds its narratives by speaking "on" (about) the real question — God and His work. Every detail, every accusation, every decision of the king in Ezra and Daniel returns "to" the temple, the reconstruction, the faithfulness to God. For us, it reminds us that our entire life must "rest" on God: our thoughts, our words, and our actions must all be directed "towards" Him and "about" His glory.

sens: a wooden piece placed on the necks of draft animals to harness them
subjugation, domination of a people by a conqueror
oppressive authority, heavy burden imposed by a master
bond of servitude or slavery
dependence, submission to a law or obligation
H5923.detail:
1. The yoke is primarily a concrete object: a wooden piece placed on the neck of two animals (often oxen or cows) to harness them together and make them work. The Bible speaks of it literally when it mentions a "cow that has never borne the yoke" (1 Samuel 6:7): it is a young beast, never subjected to labor.

2. Figuratively, the yoke refers to slavery or the political domination of a people. When the king of Babylon imposes his yoke on Judah (Jeremiah 28:2), it signifies that Israel is subject to his power and must obey. It is the image of a people bent under the authority of a conqueror.

3. The word also expresses any oppressive burden or abusive authority. King Rehoboam declares: "My father made your yoke heavy, and I will make it heavier" (1 Kings 12:14): the yoke becomes a metaphor for the heavy tax and slavery that the people must endure.

4. Broken or removed, the yoke symbolizes liberation. When the psalmist cries, "You have long since broken your yoke" (Jeremiah 2:20), he speaks of the freedom regained after oppression. The central idea is that of the weight lifted from the neck.
H5923.origine: The Hebrew word עֹל (ol) comes from a root that evokes the idea of being bent, bowed under a weight. The starting image is that of the animal's neck bending under the load of the yoke. This word belongs to an ancient Semitic family and is used in the Bible to evoke everything that subjugates and bends the back: from the concrete agricultural object to political or spiritual servitude. It is a very vivid word in biblical Hebrew, used to describe submission to a conquering king as well as obedience to God's Law.
H5923.emploi: The yoke appears 34 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the prophetic books (Jeremiah, Isaiah, Lamentations) and historical accounts. In the literal sense, it refers to the agricultural yoke that harnesses the animals (Numbers 19:2, Deuteronomy 21:3, 1 Samuel 6:7). In the political and military sense, it expresses the domination of a foreign power: Rehoboam threatens to make the people's yoke heavier (1 Kings 12:4, 12:14; 2 Chronicles 10:4, 10:14), and the prophets announce the yoke of Babylon over Judah (Jeremiah 28:2, 28:14, 30:8). Finally, the word also means subjugation to a law or obligation: Lamentations 1:14 speaks of the yoke of transgression, Hosea 11:4 of the yoke placed on Israel. The central idea remains that of a burden that bends and subjugates.
H5923.portee: The yoke reminds the believer that slavery and oppression are realities that God sees and judges. The Bible continually shows that God breaks unjust yokes and liberates enslaved peoples (Isaiah 10:27). This word also invites Christians to recognize which yokes oppress them spiritually—guilt, fear, legalism—and to seek freedom in God. Conversely, some yokes come from God Himself for our good: obedience to His laws carries us rather than crushes us.

sens: to place someone in a superior position, to appoint them as chief or responsible
to be above, to dominate
H5924.detail:
1. This word means to place someone or something in a high position, particularly in authority. In Daniel 6:2, King Darius "sets" three officials over his satraps: he places them above them to supervise and control. The image is that of elevating someone to give them power over others.
2. More broadly, the word expresses the idea of being above, dominating, or surpassing. It describes a relationship of superiority or preeminence between two things or people.
H5924.origine: This Aramaic word is the form of the Hebrew preposition עַל (al), which literally means "on" or "above." The Aramaic suffix slightly changes the form, but the fundamental meaning remains the same: to express a spatial or figurative position of elevation and domination. This preposition is very common in the Hebrew Bible with the same basic meaning.
H5924.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 6:2, where it is used to describe the action of King Darius. It means precisely "to appoint someone to a position of responsibility, to place above." In this political context, the king elevates Daniel and two other men to oversee the administration of his empire. The word emphasizes the exercise of royal authority and the establishment of a governmental hierarchy.
H5924.portee: This passage shows how earthly authority is exercised through chains of responsibility and oversight. For the believer, it reminds us that all human authority is ultimately subject to God's will: even when a king appoints leaders to maintain order, it is God who orchestrates events and protects His faithful servants like Daniel.

sens: man of the tribe of Asher during the divided monarchy
H5925.detail: Ulla is a man of the tribe of Asher, mentioned only once in the Bible. He was the son of Zophah and the father of three children: Arach, Hanniel, and Ritsja (1 Chronicles 7:39). He belongs to a genealogy of Asherites recorded during the period when the kingdoms of Israel and Judah were divided.
H5925.origine: The name Ulla means "yoke" in Hebrew, evoking the image of the yoke that binds together. It is a simple Semitic name borne by this ancestor of Asher, of whom we know little detail other than his place in the tribal genealogy.
H5925.emploi: Ulla appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 7:39, in the midst of a genealogical list of the sons of Asher. This passage enumerates the descendants of Asher and places Ulla as the son of Zophah, father of a lineage that marked the tribe. The unique mention reflects the importance given to tribal genealogies in the books of Chronicles, which preserve the memory of the families of Israel.

sens: To move upward, to climb
To go from one place to another heading upward (place, mountain, altar)
To progress, advance, make one's way
To grow, push, rise (plants, water)
To appear, emerge, manifest
To offer in sacrifice, present to God
H5927G.detail:
1. Physical movement upward: the action of climbing or rising. Example: "A mist rose from the earth" (Genesis 2:6), describing water rising from the ground to the sky.
2. Travel or movement that involves a geographical ascent or a journey to a specific place. For example, Moses and Aaron "went up to the mountain of Hor" (Numbers 20:27), or Benaiah "went up" to strike Joab (1 Kings 2:34). The word suggests a change of location with effort or intention.
3. To advance, depart, walk toward a destination or action. "Go up and attack Ramoth in Gilead" (2 Chronicles 18:14) means "go forward, attack".
4. Natural growth: plants that grow, water that rises. The image is one of life rising from the ground.
5. Appearance or manifestation: something that emerges or becomes visible. It conveys the idea of movement from a hidden state to light.
6. Offering to God: to present a sacrifice at the altar. This is the religious and spiritual sense of the word, related to worship and dependence on God.
H5927G.origine: The Hebrew verb עָלָה (alah) primarily means "to go up" or "to ascend." It is a very ancient word, rooted in the physical image of ascent. In Hebrew, this root is found in names like עוֹלָה (ola), the offering that "ascends" to God, or in עֶלְיוֹן (Elyon), "the Most High." The word has gained figurative meanings: wherever there is movement, progression, or presentation to God, this root is found. It appears more than 560 times in the Old Testament, highlighting its importance in biblical thought.
H5927G.emploi: The verb "to ascend" is extremely frequent in the Hebrew Bible (over 560 occurrences). It is primarily used to describe physical movements: ascending a mountain (Exodus 19:3, 24:12), leaving Egypt (Jeremiah 2:6), climbing stairs or a structure. It is also encountered in natural processes: water that rises (Exodus 7:28, 8:1-2), plants that grow. In a religious and cultic context, the word takes on a sacred dimension: one "ascends" to the altar to offer a sacrifice, or one "ascends" before the Lord to pray and present oneself to Him. Finally, it can express the idea of advancing or progressing in a project or conflict: ascending to war, ascending to attack. This versatility shows that the word unites all areas of human life under the image of movement upward and toward God.
H5927G.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that every movement can have a vertical dimension: we do not live only horizontally, in earthly space, but always in the presence of God who is above. The sacrifices that "ascend" to the Lord teach that our offerings, prayers, and service must be directed toward Him. Spiritually, "to ascend" also invites growth: like plants that grow and rise, the believer is called to progress in faith. It is a word of hope: even when we go through the desert or trials, we advance, we ascend toward God's promise.

sens: To go upward, to move in height
To bring out, take, lead elsewhere
To place, arrange something in position
Offering, sacrifice presented to God
To excel, surpass, dominate
H5927H.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to physically move upward or to climb: to ascend a mountain, a hill, or a staircase. It is the concrete ascent of terrain or a structure. Example: in Genesis 37:28, one "brings up" Joseph from the pit where he had fallen.
2. The word also denotes the action of bringing out or taking someone from a place: to lead, to take, to depart together. In Jeremiah 23:7, God "brings up" the children of Israel from the land of Egypt means He liberates them and leads them out.
3. To place or arrange something in position, especially in a solemn or ritual manner: to light lamps, to install an object. In Numbers 8:2, Aaron "places" the lamps on the lampstand.
4. In worship, "to bring up" an offering or a sacrifice means to present it to God, to offer it solemnly. This meaning extends to any oblation raised toward God.
5. Figuratively, the word can mean to excel or surpass someone: to be superior. It conveys the idea that one who ascends above is above.
H5927H.origine: The Hebrew root expresses upward vertical movement. The verb appears in several forms: the simple action ("to ascend"), the causative action ("to cause to ascend," "to elevate"), and the passive form ("to be carried up"). This image of upward movement naturally extends to the spiritual and metaphorical realm: what ascends to God is an offering, what rises is exalted. It is one of the most frequently used verbs in the Hebrew Old Testament.
H5927H.emploi: This word appears 146 times in the provided biblical usages, from Genesis to the prophetic and historical books. The concrete sense (to ascend, to climb) is the most common: the people ascend to Jerusalem, they come up from Egypt, they go up a mountain. A ritual and cultic usage is omnipresent: offerings are brought up, sacred objects are placed (the lamps of the lampstand). The verb is also used to mean "to bring out" or "to lead" in the sense of liberation or extraction. In historical and prophetic narratives, it describes the movements of peoples, the displacement of sacred objects, and political or military actions. The context always clarifies whether the movement is spatial, ritual, or figurative.
H5927H.portee: For the Christian reader, this verb reminds us that God "brings up" His people, meaning He liberates and leads them. The offering "brought up" to God expresses the love and devotion of the people toward Him: it is an image of what rises from the heart to God. The language of upward movement also speaks to faith: what ascends to God is accepted, what is elevated by God is honored. This image will be echoed in the New Testament to speak of the ascension of Christ and the elevation of the believer toward God.

sens: To bring an offering, a gift presented to God on an altar
To present to God a victim to honor His name or obtain His forgiveness
To regularly bring offerings according to the prescriptions of the law
A whole burnt offering that ascends in smoke to God
H5927I.detail:
1. The verb primarily evokes the physical action of bringing something up to heaven: one elevates a victim (an animal) on an altar and burns it, so that the smoke rises to God. Noah did this after the Flood: "he took of every clean animal and of every clean bird, and offered burnt offerings on the altar" (Genesis 8:20).
2. The word designates the complete act of presenting an offering to God to honor Him or to seek His forgiveness and favor. Solomon, after his divine dream, "offered burnt offerings and sacrifices of thanksgiving" to thank the Lord (1 Kings 3:15).
3. This verb is also used for the regular and obligatory offerings prescribed by the Law: the priests were to "continually offer before the Lord all the burnt offerings... on the Sabbaths, on the new moons, and on the feasts" (1 Chronicles 23:31).
4. The term can specifically refer to the burnt offering, the victim entirely consumed by fire, which is the most solemn and complete type of offering.
H5927I.origine: The Hebrew verb עָלָה comes from a root that primarily means "to go up, to ascend." The basic image is that of ascent: one brings the offering up to God, either by carrying it to the top of the altar or (for the burnt offering) by allowing it to be consumed and rise in smoke to heaven. This upward movement reflects respect, worship, and the offering of the heart turned toward God. The same verb can simply mean "to go up, to climb" (a staircase, a mountain) or "to approach" (someone), but in the religious context, it acquires the specific meaning of "to present an offering."
H5927I.emploi: The verb appears more than eighty times in the Bible, especially in the historical books and the Psalms. It is regularly used for voluntary offerings (Noah, Abraham, Solomon, Job offer sacrifices), for the obligatory rites of the Law (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers), and for the actions of kings and priests during major feasts or temple consecrations. It is also found when a believer commits by a vow to offer a sacrifice (like Jephthah in Judges 11:31). The context is almost always solemn: the offering seals a covenant, repairs a fault, honors God, or seeks His blessing. The usages show that this practice was at the heart of Israelite piety and the relationship with God.
H5927I.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that the Old Testament viewed the offering as a concrete means of turning to God, recognizing His lordship, and seeking His grace. For the evangelical Christian, it evokes Christ's sacrifice on the cross, the final and perfect offering that renders all others obsolete. Meditating on these ancient burnt offerings helps to understand the depth of what Jesus accomplished by shedding His blood for us. It is also an invitation to offer our own lives to God, not through animals and fire, but through a consecration of the heart and a life of service.

sens: To move upward, in altitude or direction
To advance against an enemy to attack or fight
To grow, germinate, develop naturally
To be elevated, exalted, surpass
To be brought, presented, offered
H5927J.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to move upward, to climb a slope or mountain, or to ascend. It is the opposite of descending. For example: in Jeremiah 6:4-5, the enemy "goes up" to attack the city, which also means "advances" or "marches" against it (the aspect of ascent can signify military approach).
2. In a military sense, "to go up" means to direct oneself toward someone to fight, to launch an offensive. In Joshua 22:12, the assembly of Israel prepares to "go up against" the tribes of the east, meaning to march armed against them for war.
3. For vegetation, the word describes natural growth: the plant "goes up," germinates, and grows. It is the image of a life force rising from the ground.
4. Figuratively, "to go up" expresses exaltation, being elevated in dignity or power, surpassing others. This evokes a spiritual ascent or promotion.
5. Finally, "to go up" can mean "to bring" or "to present," notably the offerings that one "brings up" to God at the temple, or the people that one "brings" before a judge (Ezekiel 16:40: one "brings" the crowd against someone).
H5927J.origine: The Hebrew root 'lh' evokes the fundamental idea of "to rise" and "to go up." It is very ancient and common in Hebrew. The word has several grammatical forms: the simple form (Qal) means "to go up" in a neutral sense; the passive form (Niphal) means "to be elevated"; the causative form (Hiphil) means "to cause to go up" or "to bring." The military context where the word means "to attack" or "to advance against" likely results from the image of an army that "goes up" toward the opposing city or region.
H5927J.emploi: The verb "to go up" appears 11 times in these usages. It primarily designates military movement, organized attack: Joshua 22:12 and 22:33 show Israel ready to "go up" armed against the eastern tribes; Jeremiah 6:4-5 and 51:27 describe the enemy who "goes up" to destroy Jerusalem. In Ezekiel 16:40 and 23:46, one "brings" or "advances" crowds to attack. These usages show that the verb, in a warrior context, means "to march against," "to advance militarily," "to launch an offensive." The word always retains the idea of directed movement and hostile intent.
H5927J.portee: This word reminds the reader how the Bible speaks of war: not as a spontaneous act, but as an organized movement, with intention and preparation. The image of "going up" also suggests a form of predation: one rises to strike. For the believer, this sheds light on how the Bible views conflict: it does not obscure it, but describes it without glorifying it, inviting to seek peace rather than confrontation, as the assembly of Israel in Joshua 22:33 ultimately renounces war.

sens: To move upward
To go to a place or a person
To mate (for animals)
To grow, to develop
To appear, to manifest
To be superior, to surpass
H5927K.detail:
1. To move upward, to climb a slope or height. This is the basic meaning: one ascends from a low place to a high place. In 1 Kings 12:18, King Rehoboam "ascends" onto a chariot to flee, which means to get on it and leave quickly.

2. To go to a place, a person, or a situation; to head somewhere with intention. The verb describes a directed movement, often accompanied by a nuance of departure or escape.

3. To mate, referring to male animals. In Genesis 31:10, the male goats "cover" the ewes when they come into heat: the Hebrew verb literally describes the action of the male mounting the female.

4. To grow, to sprout, to push upward, referring to vegetation or natural phenomena. The image is that of a gradual ascent from the ground.

5. To rise, to appear, referring to the movement of waves or the course of celestial bodies. In Psalms 107:26, the sailors "rise" to the heavens when the waves lift them.

6. To be superior, to surpass someone else. The figurative sense: one who "ascends" above others surpasses them in strength or honor.
H5927K.origine: The verb הָלַע (alah) comes from a very ancient root evoking upward movement. It is found in many Hebrew and Aramaic words related to ascent and rising. In Genesis 31, this same verb is also used to describe animal mating, as the image of "mounting" naturally applies to reproductive behavior. Ancient Greek takes up this verb in the Greek Old Testament to translate the same realities: physical ascent, movement to a place, and in some cases, mating.
H5927K.emploi: This verb is among the most frequent in biblical Hebrew. It first appears with its concrete meaning: to move upward or to a place (as in 1 Kings 12:18 and Jeremiah 46:4, where one ascends on a chariot or horseback). In Psalms 107:26, it describes the waves that rise. It also takes on a specialized meaning in Genesis 31:10 and 31:12, where it designates the mating of male goats with ewes: the male "covers" or "mounts" the female. In religious contexts, the verb can denote the action of "ascending" to God or to the temple. Its variants (passive, causative) allow for expressions like "to be lifted up," "to cause to ascend," "to offer" (notably in sacrifice).
H5927K.portee: This word reminds believers that life consists of upward movements and descents: circumstances make us "ascend" or "descend." In particular, "ascending" to God or to the temple is a major biblical theme: it represents the approach of the holy, the movement of the heart turning toward the Lord. Understanding this verb helps grasp the recurring image of spiritual pilgrimage and the aspiration for communion with God.

sens: Physical movement upward: to ascend, to climb, to rise
The appearance of the sun on the horizon: dawn, daybreak, daylight
Departure, retreat, moving away from a place
Growth, flourishing: to push, to sprout
Presentation, offering: to bring before God
Excellence, superiority: to surpass, to prevail
H5927L.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is that of vertical movement: to go upward, to ascend, to climb. It is the movement of the body rising, as when Jacob rises after his night struggle (Genesis 32:24).
2. The word also designates dawn, the moment when the sun rises on the horizon: it is the "rising" of the sun, the appearance of daylight (Genesis 32:26: "the dawn rises"). This meaning naturally follows from the first: one watches the sun ascend in the sky.
3. By extension, the word can express departure, retreat, leaving a place. Those who "rise" early in the morning set out (Joshua 6:15: "they rose early in the morning").
4. Applied to plants and living beings, it means to grow, to push, to flourish: vegetation that "rises" toward the sky.
5. In a religious context, the word can mean to bring an offering, to present it to God. It conveys the idea of "lifting" something to give it.
6. Finally, it can express the idea of excelling, surpassing, being superior to something or someone.
H5927L.origine: The Hebrew word עָלָה (alah) comes from a very ancient root that fundamentally evokes the idea of upward movement. Its initial image is that of the rising sun and everything that ascends. The word has given rise to several grammatical forms: some reinforce the idea of ascending (causative: "to cause to ascend"), while others add the idea of reflexivity ("to rise oneself"). It is a very common word in the Old Testament, expressing both simple everyday gestures and spiritual realities.
H5927L.emploi: The word עָלָה appears more than seven hundred times in the Old Testament. In the provided usages, it first designates dawn, the moment when the day rises: it is "the dawn that rises" (Genesis 32:26) or "at dawn" (Joshua 6:15). It also signifies the action of rising, standing up, or setting out: "They rose early in the morning" (1 Samuel 9:26), "Rise up" (Genesis 19:15). The word is used to express the transition from rest to action, or from night to day. In the Bible, it also carries a strong spiritual weight: "ascending" to God, "offering" to God (particularly in worship), or "excelling" in wisdom or strength. Depending on the context and grammatical form, the precise meaning varies, but the idea of upward movement remains central.
H5927L.portee: Understanding this word helps the reader grasp how the Bible views time and action. Dawn is never neutral: it is a moment of clarity, renewal, often of decision or judgment. When the text says "at dawn," it emphasizes the urgency or solemnity of a moment. The "rising" can also spiritually evoke resurrection and renewal: what ascends transcends what is low. For the believer, this word reminds that to "rise" is also to respond to God's call, to set out toward Him.

sens: To bring back to the mouth and chew again what has already been swallowed
To be an animal that ruminates
To bring up, to regurgitate (the primary sense of the verb before its specialization)
H5927M.detail:
1. To ruminate is the natural process by which certain animals (cows, goats, camels) bring back what they have swallowed to chew it again, then swallow it again. Leviticus 11:3 and Deuteronomy 14:6 describe the criteria for purity: "You may eat any animal that has a split hoof, is cloven-footed, and ruminates."
2. The verb also simply serves to designate an animal that possesses this ability, regardless of the action itself: Leviticus 11:4 states that one shall not eat "those that ruminate only, or that have a split hoof only," meaning: the animals that ruminate but do not have a split hoof.
H5927M.origine: The verb עָלָה (alah) first means "to ascend, to rise up": its root evokes upward movement. Applied to the digestion of ruminants, it precisely describes what "rises" from the stomach to the mouth. It is the image of upward movement that has given the verb this specialized physiological sense.
H5927M.emploi: This verb appears only 7 times in the Bible, always in the dietary laws of Leviticus (chapters 11) and Deuteronomy (chapter 14). It always designates the specific ability of certain animals to ruminate. These passages establish the rules of ritual purity: an animal was declared pure if it met two conditions — having a split hoof AND ruminating. The camel, the hare, and the rock badger, although they ruminate, are deemed impure because they do not have a split hoof. The word remains always in this legislative and technical context.
H5927M.portee: These dietary laws of Leviticus and Deuteronomy teach the people of Israel to discern between the pure and the impure, and to obey commandments whose profound wisdom remains partly veiled. For the Christian, these ancient rules show how God guides His children with precision in every detail of daily life, even the simplest ones.

sens: Sacrifice where the entire animal is offered to God by fire
Burnt offering of worship that ascends to God
Act of total consecration of oneself
H5928.detail:
1. The burnt offering is an animal sacrifice where the priest kills the animal (bulls, rams, lambs), dismembers it, and then completely burns it on the altar. Nothing remains except for the ashes. In Ezra 6:9, the king orders that animals and provisions necessary for these burnt offerings to the God of heaven be provided daily to the priests of Jerusalem.
2. What ascends from the sacrifice — the smoke and the aroma — is a fragrance that rises to the throne of God. The Hebrew word עֹלָה "olah" comes from a root meaning "to ascend," which emphasizes that the entire offering rises to the Most High.
3. The burnt offering expresses total abandonment, unreserved consecration: the consumed animal symbolizes the soul that gives itself entirely to its Creator. It is an act of pure worship, even before the forgiveness of sins.
H5928.origine: This Aramaic word עֲלָת "alah" is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew word עֹלָה "olah" which appears more than 80 times in the Old Testament. The root עלה means "to ascend": the sacrifice ascends to God. The Aramaic "alah" is found in Ezra 6:9, a passage that speaks of a decree from King Darius allowing worship at the rebuilt temple; it is in Aramaic that certain sections of Ezra and Daniel are written, the parts concerning relations with the Persian power.
H5928.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament in the provided Aramaic-Hebrew (Ezra 6:9), but the Hebrew word "olah" is extremely frequent in Leviticus (which provides the detailed ritual), in Numbers, and in the historical books. The burnt offering is among the five major sacrifices of the Mosaic law. In Ezra 6:9, after the return from captivity, the Jews resume the daily burnt offering at the rebuilt temple. It is a regular act of worship, central to the religious life of Israel, a sign of dependence and worship toward God.
H5928.portee: For the Christian, the burnt offering speaks of total consecration to God: it is an image of what the Apostle Paul calls "presenting your bodies as a living sacrifice" (Romans 12:1). The New Testament teaches that Jesus Christ is the great Burnt Offering, the perfect sacrifice offered once for all. Understanding what this sacrifice was helps the believer grasp the depth of Christ's gift and calls them to a consecration of their entire being.

sens: The green, flat part of a plant or tree
The entirety of a tree's leaves; the foliage
A branch or twig bearing leaves
The fragility and instability of what passes quickly
The prosperity and spiritual life of the righteous
H5929.detail:
1. The leaf is the green, flat part of the tree, such as when Noah sees an olive leaf in the dove's beak, a sign that the earth is reborn after the flood (Genesis 8:11), or as Isaiah describes the leaves that fall from the vine and the fig tree (Isaiah 34:4).
2. The word also refers to the entire foliage of a tree, the collection of leaves that covers it: the righteous flourish like foliage, says Proverbs 11:28, evoking abundant and lasting life.
3. By leaf, one also means a twig, a branch adorned with leaves, as when at the Feast of Tabernacles, branches and leafy boughs are cut (Nehemiah 8:15).
4. The leaf becomes an image of fragility: it trembles at the slightest wind and falls easily, as shown in Job 13:25 ("Will you frighten a leaf driven to and fro?") or Leviticus 26:36 where the sound of a leaf shaken terrifies sinners.
5. The verdant foliage of the righteous symbolizes eternal life and blessing: he who meditates on the Law day and night "will be like a tree planted by streams of water, which yields its fruit in its season, and its leaf does not wither" (Psalms 1:3).
H5929.origine: The Hebrew word עָלֶה comes from a root related to the idea of ascending, rising: the leaf is what rises and elevates on the plant. In the Old Testament, this word first denotes the leaf in a simple botanical sense, before acquiring figurative nuances of fragility and life. The Hebrew word is a common noun, very ancient, related to observable and daily nature.
H5929.emploi: The word appears 13 times in the Old Testament, especially in wisdom poetry (Job, Proverbs, Psalms) and in the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel). From the first concrete uses (Genesis 3:7: the fig leaves that Adam and Eve made for themselves), a symbolic charge quickly adds. In passages of decay or judgment (Isaiah 34:4, Jeremiah 8:13), falling leaves signify ruin and extinction. Conversely, in texts of blessing and wisdom (Psalms 1:3, Proverbs 11:28, Jeremiah 17:8), the verdant foliage represents spiritual prosperity and abundance of life. This progression of meaning shows how the Bible takes advantage of the natural image to speak of spiritual destinies.
H5929.portee: The leaf teaches two complementary lessons. On one hand, its fragility reminds us that without God, all that shines collapses: wealth, strength, the plans of the wicked vanish like leaves in the wind. On the other hand, the foliage of the righteous prospers, indicating that one who is rooted in the word of God bears fruit and remains stable: their life is fruitful and enduring. This simple image invites the reader to choose where they root their trust.

sens: sacrifice where the animal is entirely consumed by fire on the altar
offering of an animal presented to God to obtain His forgiveness or favor
act of total devotion to God
H5930A.detail:
1. The burnt offering is a sacrifice where the offered animal — bull, ram, goat, bird according to the wealth of the worshiper — is completely burned on the altar. No part is kept for the priest's table: everything ascends to God in smoke. Noah "offered burnt offerings" (Genesis 8:20), meaning he burned on the altar the pure animals he had reserved.
2.
