H5984H.portee: The Ammonites remind the Christian reader that God has established boundaries between peoples, and that marital alliances with idolatrous nations exposed Israel to religious unfaithfulness. The example of Solomon, seduced by the deities of the Ammonites, illustrates how political compromises can corrupt faith. It is a lesson on the necessity of remaining separate from what distances one from God.

sens: prophet of Israel in the 8th century B.C.
H5986.detail: Amos is a prophet of the Lord who ministered in the Northern Kingdom (Israel) during the time of King Jeroboam II. Originally from Tekoa, a village in Judah near Bethlehem, he was a shepherd by trade and a sycamore fig farmer (7:14), not a professional prophet, but called by God to announce His judgment on Israel. The Lord granted him visions where he saw God's plumb line set in the midst of the people: an image of divine judgment that measures justice (7:8). His prophetic words denouncing the sins of Israel provoked hostility from the priest Amaziah of Bethel, who attempted to drive him away (7:12), but Amos stood firm in his calling (7:10-11). His name means "burden," reflecting the weight of the message of condemnation he bore.
H5986.origine: The name Amos literally means "burden" or "one who carries a burden" in Hebrew, an evocative image of the heavy prophetic message he was charged to proclaim. Amos did not come from the prophetic class: he was a simple man, directly called by God to leave his work as a shepherd to become the Lord's spokesperson to Israel.
H5986.emploi: Amos appears seven times in the provided texts, all in the book that bears his name. He is first introduced in Amos 1:1 as one of the shepherds of Tekoa, the author of the visions and prophecies that form the book. In chapter 7, we see his interaction with the Lord: God shows him visions of judgment (7:8) and recognizes him as a prophet despite the opposition from religious authorities. Amaziah, priest of Bethel, denounces him to the king as a conspirator (7:10) and attempts to send him back to Judah (7:12), calling him "man of visions." Amos responds with humility and firmness: he is neither a professional prophet nor the son of a prophet, but a shepherd chosen by God (7:14). His central message was that the Lord would set the level of justice in the midst of Israel and would no longer pardon (7:8-11).
H5986.portee: Amos reminds the believer that God calls simple men, without established religious status, to faithfully announce His word. His example shows that true obedience to God takes precedence over comfort, prestige, or human acceptance: he chose to obey the Lord rather than yield to the threats of authorities. For us, he remains a model of prophetic courage and bravery in the face of opposition.

sens: priest who returned from exile with Zerubbabel
H5987.detail: 1. Amok is a priest mentioned during the return from exile to Jerusalem, at the time of Zerubbabel. He is listed among the leaders of the priests who returned from Babylon (Nehemiah 12:7), indicating that he held a position of responsibility among the restored clergy. Later, the mention of Eber as his successor or descendant in the priestly function (Nehemiah 12:20) indicates that his office continued in his lineage.
H5987.origine: The name Amok literally means "deep being" in Hebrew, but its exact meaning in the context of personal identity remains mysterious. It is a proper name attested only for this individual in the Scriptures, during the period of restoration of worship in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile.
H5987.emploi: Amok appears twice in the book of Nehemiah, both in chapter 12, which lists the priests and Levites who returned with Zerubbabel. In Nehemiah 12:7, he is named among the leaders of the priests contemporary with Joshua the high priest. In Nehemiah 12:20, a generation later, Eber is mentioned as the one who bears the responsibility that belonged to Amok, which testifies to the succession of priestly offices within the families of priests.

sens: spy sent by Moses to explore Canaan, representing the tribe of Dan
H5988G.detail: Ammiel is one of the twelve men chosen by Moses to scout the land of Canaan before Israel's entry. He represents the tribe of Dan and is the son of Gemalli (Numbers 13:12). Like the other spies, he returned with a report on the promised land, but this report was a bad faith report that discouraged the people and provoked the anger of God.
H5988G.origine: The name Ammiel literally means "my kinsman is God" or "my people is God," composed of two elements: "ammi" (my people) and "el" (God). It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God, which was common in Hebrew onomastics to express a personal relationship with the divine.
H5988G.emploi: Ammiel appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 13:12, where he is named among the twelve spies. He is identified as the representative of the tribe of Dan, son of Gemalli. Although Scripture does not report his exact words, he participated in the spies' report that refused to accept God's promise regarding Canaan. According to the narrative in Numbers 14, this unbelief led to a plague that killed ten of the twelve spies for their bad report.
H5988G.portee: Ammiel illustrates how unbelief in the promises of God carries serious consequences. Even having seen divine wonders in Egypt and in the desert, even having received a direct mission from God, the absence of faith resulted in judgment. His story reminds readers that seeing is not believing, and that only trust in God's word, despite apparent adverse circumstances, leads to life.

sens: Father of Makir of Lo-Debar, a man of Gilead during the time of King David
H5988H.detail: Ammiel is a notable from the region of Gilead, father of Makir. Makir is known for having welcomed Mephibosheth, the son of Saul, into his home after Saul's death (2 Samuel 9:4-5). Later, when King David fled Jerusalem during Absalom's rebellion, Makir, son of Ammiel, is among those who come to provide for the king in Mahanaim (2 Samuel 17:27). The name Ammiel means "my kinsman is God" — a confession of faith in divine protection.
H5988H.origine: The Hebrew name עַמִּיאֵל is composed of עַם ("people, kinsman") and אֵל ("God"). It expresses a familial relationship under divine guardianship: God is the one who protects the clan or kin. It is a typical theophoric name from the royal period, where the names of notable families displayed their trust in God.
H5988H.emploi: Ammiel appears three times in the account of the second book of Samuel. He is the father of Makir of Lo-Debar, a city in Gilead east of the Jordan. Makir first welcomes Mephibosheth, son of Saul, into his home — an act of compassion since Saul and his sons were dead and David had become king (2 Samuel 9:4-5). Then, during David's flight from the rebellion of his son Absalom, Makir, son of Ammiel, is mentioned among the great notables who come to aid the exiled king in Mahanaim (2 Samuel 17:27). Ammiel himself does not act; only his son Makir appears in the living history of David.

sens: son of Obed-Edom, Levite gatekeeper of the temple during the time of the united monarchy
H5988I.detail: Ammiel is a man from the tribe of Levi who lived during the time of the united monarchy (the time of King David and his successors). He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 26:5, where he is identified as the sixth son of Obed-Edom. He served as a gatekeeper of the temple, an important role entrusted to the Levites to guard access to the house of God and maintain order in worship. Obed-Edom, his father, was also a renowned temple gatekeeper, whom God had particularly blessed with many sons.
H5988I.origine: The name Ammiel means "my kinsman is God" or "my ally is God" in Hebrew (composed of *ammi* = "my people/my kinsman" and *el* = "God"). It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the name of God, expressing the trust that the parent who gave it had in the protection and covenant of the Lord. Several men bore this name in the Bible, but this one is specifically identified by his relation to Obed-Edom.
H5988I.emploi: Ammiel is mentioned only once in the preserved biblical text: in 1 Chronicles 26:5. At this point, the author of the book of Chronicles lists the sons of Obed-Edom who inherited the role of gatekeeper of the temple during the united monarchy. The context shows that this Levitical family had received a holy responsibility from the Lord and that God had blessed Obed-Edom by giving him several sons to fulfill this role. Ammiel thus represents a generation of faithful servants of the temple of the Lord.

sens: father of Bathsheba
man of the time of the united monarchy
H5988J.detail: Ammiel is the father of Bathsheba, the wife of King David. This is the only direct use of the name in the Bible: in 1 Chronicles 3:5, he is explicitly named as the father of "Bath-Shua" (another name for Bathsheba). He is also encountered under the name Eliam in 2 Samuel 11:3, where the text designates him as "the father of Bathsheba." He belonged to the time of the united monarchy, under the reign of David.
H5988J.origine: The name Ammiel means "my kinsman is God" or "my relative is God" in Hebrew: it is formed from two elements, "am" (kinsman, people) and "el" (God). It is a characteristic theophoric name from the biblical period, expressing trust in God as the protector of the family.
H5988J.emploi: Ammiel is mentioned only once in the Bible under this name: in 1 Chronicles 3:5, where he is identified as the father of Bathsheba, mother of Solomon. However, the same person also appears in 2 Samuel 11:3 under the name Eliam. He is a figure from the time of David, father of the woman with whom the king commits adultery.

sens: chief of the tribe of Ephraim at the time of the Exodus, father of Elishama
ancestor in the genealogy of Ephraim
H5989G.detail: 1. Ammihud is an Ephraimite who holds a position of responsibility during the exodus from Egypt: he is the father of Elishama, who is designated as prince (chief) of the tribe of Ephraim (Numbers 1:10). His son is tasked with commanding the army of Ephraim and participating in the inauguration of the Tabernacle with offerings (Numbers 7:48). 2. Ammihud also appears in the genealogical lineage of Ephraim, son of Laadan, who is himself an ancestor of Elishama (1 Chronicles 7:26). He represents one of the intermediate generations of this tribe during the desert period and the beginning of the settlement in the Promised Land.
H5989G.origine: The Hebrew name Ammihud literally means "my kinsman is majesty (glory)." It is composed of two elements: *am* (people, kinsman) and *hud*, which evokes greatness or glory. This name reflects Israelite faith: the God of the fathers, who is the kinsman of the people, is honored for His majesty and power.
H5989G.emploi: Ammihud appears six times in the biblical text, always in passages from the Pentateuch and Chronicles related to the organization of Israel during the Exodus. The majority of mentions (Numbers 1:10; 2:18; 7:48; 7:53; 10:22) designate him as the father of Elishama, prince of the tribe of Ephraim, in the census lists and the accounts of the offerings of the Tabernacle. A final mention (1 Chronicles 7:26) places him in the genealogical succession of Ephraim. Ammihud is never the subject of an action: it is always through his son that he appears in the history of Israel.
H5989G.portee: Ammihud reminds us that the great leaders of Israel — even the princes of the twelve tribes — are integrated into genealogies that trace back to the ancestors of the people. His role as the father of the chief Elishama shows how authority is passed down within the families of Israel and how God structures His people through lines of leaders. This name, whose meaning celebrates divine majesty, invites the believer to recognize that each generation of Israel is woven into a history shaped by the power and glory of God.

sens: man of the tribe of Simeon, father of Shemuel
one of the five princes that Moses chose to divide the territory of Canaan
H5989H.detail:
1. Ammihud is a man of the tribe of Simeon, father of Shemuel (Numbers 34:20). His name means "my relative is majesty" and expresses divine greatness.
2. In the context of the division of Canaan, Moses designates five princes to allocate the conquered lands among the tribes. Ammihud is the father of Shemuel, chosen to represent the tribe of Simeon in this crucial task (Numbers 34:20). This role shows that he came from a family of recognized leaders in his tribe.
H5989H.origine: The name Ammihud is composed of two Hebrew words: "am" (my relative, my kinsman) and "hud" (majesty, glory). It reflects the parents' trust in the greatness and majesty of God.
H5989H.emploi: Ammihud appears only once in the preserved texts: in Numbers 34:20, where he is named as the father of Shemuel, one of the five princes chosen by Moses to oversee the division of the lands of Canaan among the tribes. This unique but solemn mention places him among the trustworthy men at the decisive moment of the people's settlement in the Promised Land.

sens: Man living during the time of the Exodus and the wilderness journey
H5989I.detail: Ammihud is a name borne by several men in the Bible during the time of the Exodus and the wilderness period. The provided passage mentions him as the father of Pedahel, prince of the tribe of Naphtali (Numbers 34:28). Other Ammihuds are cited in different biblical contexts: one was the father of Elishama, chief of the tribe of Ephraim; another was the father of Shemuel of Simeon; yet another was the father of King Talmai of Geshur; and a final one descended from Judah through his son Perez. The name means "my relative is majesty," combining the idea of kinship and royal grandeur.
H5989I.origine: The name Ammihud comes from Hebrew and combines two elements: "am" (relative, people) and "hud" (referring to majesty or splendor). It is a theophoric name characteristic of the patriarchal and Mosaic period, where names often carried a declaration of faith or a relationship with the divine.
H5989I.emploi: Ammihud is a name borne by at least five different men in the Bible, all living during the time of the Exodus or shortly thereafter. In the cited passage (Numbers 34:28), he is the father of Pedahel, designated as prince of the tribe of Naphtali during the division of the promised land. Other occurrences of the name in the Bible show that it was a fairly common name among tribal leaders and prominent families, likely reflecting its prestigious character.

sens: father of Talmai, king of Geshur
H5989J.detail: Ammihur is a king of Geshur, a neighboring country to Israel, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the father of Talmai, to whom Prince Absalom fled after killing his brother Amnon (2 Samuel 13:37). It is with this maternal grandfather that David's rebellious son finds refuge and protection for three years.
H5989J.origine: The name Ammihur literally means "my people is majesty" or "my relative is majestic." This theophoric name (which contains the idea of greatness) was borne by several men in biblical Israel, including an Ephraimite during the time of the Exodus and a descendant of Judah. It is a common Semitic name from the ancient Levant.
H5989J.emploi: Ammihur appears only once in the Bible as king of Geshur, the land where Maacah, the mother of Absalom, had retreated (2 Samuel 3:3). He welcomes his grandson Absalom after the murder of Amnon, complicating the relations between David and the neighboring kingdom of Geshur. This brief mention reveals the political importance of Geshur and the dynastic alliances...

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the Exile and Return
H5989K.detail: Ammihud is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 9:4. He is the son of Omri and the father of Uthai. His name means "my relative is majesty" or "my people is glory," expressing confidence in divine greatness within the family. He appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Perez, one of the sons of Judah, during the return from Exile to Babylon, a period when the families of God's people were re-establishing themselves in the promised land.
H5989K.origine: The name Ammihud comes from Hebrew: "am" (people, relative, kinsman) and "hud" (majesty, glory). It expresses an ancient theological conviction: the link between the human family and the majesty of God. This name was borne by several important figures in Israel's history, including an Ephraimite leader at the time of the Exodus and a prince of Naphtali, all reflecting this same confidence in the divine greatness protecting the people.
H5989K.emploi: Ammihud is mentioned only once in 1 Chronicles 9:4, in the context of the return of the exiles from Babylon. He is listed in the genealogy of the families that resettled in Jerusalem after the captivity. This unique mention shows that he was a respected ancestor of the tribe of Judah, recorded among those whose descendants survived the Exile and participated in the restoration of the Jewish community.
H5989K.portee: This name reminds believers that God preserves His families and lineages even through the gravest crises, such as the Exile. The return to Jerusalem of which Ammihud is an ancestor shows that the divine promise to Judah never fades, and that each generation that re-establishes itself in faith participates in the fulfillment of God's purpose for His people.

sens: Son of Benajah, military chief under King David
H5990.detail: Ammizadab is the son of Benajah, one of the most powerful warriors during the time of King David. At the end of David's reign, the kingdom was organized into twelve military divisions that took turns ensuring defense and order. Benajah commanded the third division, and his son Ammizadab was one of the leaders of that same division (1 Chronicles 27:6), thus inheriting the military responsibility of his family.
H5990.origine: The name Ammizadab means "my people have given" or "my people have provided." It is composed of "ammi" (my people) and "zavad" (he has given, he has provided). This name reflects confidence in the provision and support of the people, a common conviction in ancient Hebrew culture.
H5990.emploi: Ammizadab appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:6. He is mentioned solely in this administrative and military context: he was one of the officers under his father Benajah during the organization of David's army. He does not appear in any other biblical story or narrative.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah, father of Nahshon
Ancestor of Jesus through the lineage of Judah
Father-in-law of Aaron
H5992G.detail:
1. Amminadab is a family chief of the tribe of Judah at the time of the Exodus from Egypt. His son Nahshon is the prince designated to represent Judah during the census and offerings to the Lord (Numbers 1:7; Numbers 7:12).

2. He is a direct ancestor of Jesus Christ according to the genealogy of Judah, appearing in the royal line leading to David and the Messiah (Ruth 4:19-20).

3. Amminadab is the father of Elishaba, who marries Aaron and becomes the mother of the future priests of Israel (Exodus 6:23). Through this marriage, he establishes a link between the tribe of Judah and the priestly family.
H5992G.origine: His name means "my people are noble" or "my relative is noble." It is a compound name that reflects the importance of kinship and nobility in Israelite culture. Amminadab belongs to the genealogy of Perez and Judah, a prestigious line in Israel's history.
H5992G.emploi: Amminadab appears nine times in Scripture, primarily in the books of Exodus and Numbers, where he is presented as the father of Nahshon, the leader of Judah during the wilderness. It is by virtue of his son that his name is mentioned: Nahshon represents Judah for the census (Numbers 1:7), sets up camp in the east (Numbers 2:3), presents the first offering at the dedication of the tabernacle (Numbers 7:12-17), and leads the march of the tribe (Numbers 10:14). Amminadab is also listed in the genealogy of Ruth (Ruth 4:19-20) and in 1 Chronicles 2:10, where he is noted as the father of Nahshon in the lineage leading to David and the Messiah.
H5992G.portee: The name Amminadab reminds us that God chooses His instruments from among human lineages. As an ancestor of Jesus through the tribe of Judah, he illustrates how the Lord has guided the history of the chosen people toward the coming of the Messiah. His connection to Aaron through the marriage of his daughter also shows how God united the prophetic and priestly functions in His plan of salvation.

sens: Leader Levite of the family of Uzziel
Member of the priestly family of the Kohathites
H5992H.detail:
1. Amminadab is a Levite leader, responsible for a group of priests and Levites from the family of Uzziel (1 Chronicles 15:10). He leads one hundred twelve of his brothers in the liturgical service of the temple, under the authority of King David.
2. He is a Levite from the lineage of Kohath, belonging to the priestly family that had specific responsibilities in the transport and care of the sacred objects of the Tabernacle and the Temple.
H5992H.origine: The name means "my kinsman is noble" or "my relative is illustrious": it designates someone belonging to a family of high rank or prestige. It is a common theophoric name in Israel, composed of Semitic elements expressing nobility and family kinship. This name reflects the social and religious importance of the person who bears it.
H5992H.emploi: Amminadab appears twice in Chronicles, only in 1 Chronicles 15. He is mentioned as the leader of the branch of Uzziel at the time when King David organizes the solemn transport of the Ark of the Covenant to Jerusalem. This is a decisive moment in the religious history of Israel: the Levites are gathered and organized for this great cultic celebration. Amminadab plays a role as the leader of the Levites from his family.

sens: Son of Kehath and father of Korah, a Levite from the tribe of Levi
H5992I.detail: Amminadab is a Levite, a member of the tribe of Levi, who lived during the time of Egypt and the desert. He is the son of Kehath and the father of Korah. The genealogy places him in the priestly lineage: he is part of the direct descendants of Levi, to whom God would later entrust the service of the Tabernacle. In 1 Chronicles 6:22, he appears in the list of generations of Levitical leaders, which shows his importance in the organization of Israel's worship.
H5992I.origine: The name Amminadab means "my people is noble" or "my kinsman is noble". It is composed of two elements: "ammi" (my people) and "nadab" (willing, noble). It is a typical theophoric name in biblical Hebrew, expressing a relationship or quality related to God or the community. The name is borne by several important figures in the genealogy of Israel.
H5992I.emploi: Amminadab appears in the priestly genealogy of the Levites. The provided usage (1 Chronicles 6:22) places him in the direct succession of Kehath, showing that he is an important link in the genealogical chain of the Levites responsible for the service of the Tabernacle. This passage lists the descendants of Levi in order of generation, indicating that Amminadab's role was that of a leader or representative of his family in the religious organization of Israel.

sens: Having a great extent from top to bottom, from the surface to the inner layers
That which is hidden, difficult to reach or understand
Secret mysteries, that which escapes ordinary understanding
H5994.detail:
1. The primary meaning is spatial: that which sinks far down, that which has much depth. It is the image of a well or water that cannot be touched from the bottom.

2. Figuratively, the word designates that which is hidden, distant from the surface and ordinary sight. It is that which requires effort or wisdom to be discovered.

3. The word is used for secret mysteries, hidden truths that only God can reveal. In Daniel 2:22, it speaks of "deep things" — the secrets of kings and the hidden future — that only God knows and can unveil.
H5994.origine: The Hebrew word עֲמִיק (amiq) comes from a root that evokes the idea of penetrating far, of sinking. The basic image is that of spatial depth. The word is infrequent in the Old Testament and carries a strong spiritual charge: it refers not to ordinary physical depth, but to that which belongs to the hidden, secret, mysterious realm.
H5994.emploi: The word appears rarely in the Hebrew Bible. In Daniel 2:22, it designates the "deep things" that God reveals to King Nebuchadnezzar through the dream and its interpretation. It is in a context where Daniel praises God for revealing hidden mysteries to princes and kings — a wisdom that mere men do not possess. The usage emphasizes that God knows and can make known what is deeply hidden.
H5994.portee: This word reminds the reader that God has access to mysteries that surpass human understanding. It invites recognition that true wisdom — the kind that penetrates secrets and the future — is a gift from God, never an ordinary human possession. For the believer, this affirms that God does not leave us in total ignorance of the meaning of events that surpass us.

sens: Bundle of cut and tied grain
Gathered assembly, compact mass
Crowd or multitude piled together
H5995.detail:
1. A sheaf is a bundle of grain that has been cut and tied together after the harvest. It is what is left behind when reaping: "Like the sheaf that falls behind the reaper, which no one gathers" (Jeremiah 9:22). The image is that of ears of grain gathered and tied into a bundle.
2. By extension, the word designates anything gathered into a compact mass, piled together. In Amos 2:13, God says: "I will crush you, as a cart crushes when loaded with sheaves" — here the sheaves are piled on the cart, forming a heavy and crushing load.
3. The word is used to describe a crowd or multitude gathered in one place. Micah 4:12 uses this image: "He gathered them like sheaves in the threshing floor" — the enemy peoples are piled together, ready to be judged, just like the sheaves of grain in the threshing floor.
H5995.origine: The word עָמִיר comes from a Hebrew root evoking the idea of binding or gathering. Its primary meaning is concrete and agricultural: it is the sheaf of wheat, the sheaf in English. The image is natural in Israel, a land of harvest: the cut grain naturally forms tied bundles that are stacked. From there, the word has enriched its figurative meaning to designate any compact gathering, any mass or crowd piled together.
H5995.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, all in the Prophets. In Jeremiah 9:22, it literally describes the ears falling behind the reaper. In Amos 2:13 and Micah 4:12, it shifts to the figurative: the sheaves become the image of a crowd or multitude gathered, often with a nuance of judgment or crushing. In Zechariah 12:6, the leaders of Judah are compared to a blazing fire "among sheaves" — here the word simply describes a combustible pile. In all cases, the image emphasizes compactness, gathering, and often the vulnerability of what is piled together.
H5995.portee: For the reader, the sheaf is a biblical image of human fragility and divine power. When God speaks of gathering enemies "like sheaves", He shows that He reduces them to helplessness, piles them up, and can annihilate them like grain. It is a reminder that man, despite his pride, is but a sheaf in the hands of God — grouped, limited, submissive. This image gives the believer assurance: God controls the peoples and history as the reaper controls his harvest.

sens: Father of the prince Ahiézer, leader of the tribe of Dan at the time of the Exodus
H5996.detail: Ammishaddai is the father of Ahiézer, who was designated as prince (leader) of the tribe of Dan during the census of the people in the desert of Sinai. His name means "my kinsman is the Almighty", expressing trust in divine protection. He appears in the texts of the book of Numbers concerning the organization of the Hebrew people and the offerings of the tabernacle.
H5996.origine: The name Ammishaddai combines two Hebrew elements: "ammi" (my people, or my kinsman) and "Shaddai" (the Almighty, one of the ancient names of God). It thus expresses a confession of faith: the one who bears this name proclaims that the Almighty God is his protector and ally.
H5996.emploi: Ammishaddai appears five times in the book of Numbers, always as the father of Ahiézer. He is mentioned during the census of the Israelites (Numbers 1:12), in the organization of the camp of the tribes (Numbers 2:25), during the offerings for the consecration of the tabernacle (Numbers 7:66, 7:71), and when the camp sets out toward the Promised Land (Numbers 10:25). Although he is never described in person, his existence confirms the genealogy of the leader of Dan and the honor given to this tribe in the divine order of the people.

sens: one who lives near oneself, one's neighbor
the person with whom one interacts in daily life
the one towards whom one has moral and legal duties
the other, any other human being that one must respect and love
H5997.detail:
1. The neighbor is primarily one who lives near you, your neighbor in a geographical sense. These are the people with whom we share space and daily life.
2. More broadly, it is one with whom we transact, we deal: a debtor (Leviticus 25:14-15), someone to whom we entrust a possession or whose possession we usurp (Leviticus 5:21). The neighbor is one whose life we intersect concretely.
3. Towards this neighbor weigh obligations: do not steal from him, do not lie about him, do not commit adultery with his wife, judge him justly (Leviticus 19:11, 19:15, 18:20). We must even correct him if we see him sinning (Leviticus 19:17).
4. By extension, it refers to any other human: the word designates humanity seen as a collection of individuals, each deserving respect and righteousness. This is why we must love our neighbor, not out of sentimentality, but in obedience to God.
H5997.origine: The Hebrew word עָמִית (amit) comes from the root עָמַד (amad), "to stand, to be near," hence "one who stands beside." It is the technical term for designating interpersonal relationships in Israelite law: this word is found throughout the holiness code of Leviticus, which regulates the communal life of Israel. Its later Hebrew equivalent is ישִׁיב, but amit dominates the written Torah.
H5997.emploi: This word appears 10 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in Leviticus (9 occurrences: 5:21, 18:20, 19:11, 19:15, 19:17, 24:19, 25:14, 25:15, 25:17), and once in Zechariah 13:7. It is the key word of the moral law of Leviticus 19, the heart of the holiness code: you shall love your neighbor, you shall not deceive him, you shall not steal from him. Each usage concerns a concrete relationship and a legal or moral obligation — fair trade, respect for property, marital fidelity, justice in judgments, fraternal correction. One usage (Leviticus 5:21) uses "fraud" instead of "neighbor," as it is a context where the emphasis is on lying rather than on the relationship.
H5997.portee: The word "neighbor" raises a fundamental question: whom should I love and respect? The Law of Israel answers: the one who surrounds you, the one with whom you exchange. It is not a sentimental love, but a practical justice: honesty in business, chastity, truth, impartiality in court. To love your neighbor is primarily to let him live, to treat him according to God's justice. This word invites every reader to see in those around him — neighbor, colleague, stranger — someone towards whom he has concrete duties.

sens: To perform physical or mental work with effort and perseverance
To produce a result, a work through one's labor
To take pains, to exert oneself to accomplish a task
The fruit or result of the work accomplished
H5998.detail:
1. To perform physical or mental work with effort and perseverance: this is the primary meaning, the action of continuous labor. In Proverbs 16:26, the one who works "works for himself," meaning that his labor sustains and nourishes him.

2. To produce a result, a work through one's labor: the word also encompasses the work that arises from this effort. In Ecclesiastes 2:11, the Preacher has "considered all the works" that his "hands had made, and the toil he had taken to execute them."

3. To take pains, to exert oneself to accomplish a task: this emphasizes the effort and fatigue inherent in work. In Ecclesiastes 1:3, the text asks what "advantage does man gain from all the toil he undertakes?"

4. The fruit or result of the work accomplished: the word can also refer to what one obtains through work. In Ecclesiastes 2:19, the "fruit of my wisdom" speaks of the result that work and reflection produce.
H5998.origine: The Hebrew root עָמַל (amal) evokes the idea of intense effort and fatigue. It is associated with toil and sweat, the primary image being that of the body exhausting itself at work. Related words in Hebrew denote pain, suffering, and labor, all revolving around this same notion of painful effort. The verb expresses work less as a simple activity than as a trial.
H5998.emploi: The verb appears about ten times in the Bible, especially in the wisdom literature like Ecclesiastes, where it recites one of humanity's great questions: what is the point of toiling if everything is vanity? In Psalms 127:1, it illustrates the futility of human construction without God's blessing. In Proverbs 16:26, it affirms that work provides for needs. In Ecclesiastes, it returns as a melancholic leitmotif: the author "works," "takes pains," and asks what profit results from it. The context varies from practical affirmation (work nourishes) to philosophical questioning (does work have meaning?). In Jonah 4:10, it even describes the plant that "grew" in a night without Jonah cultivating it.
H5998.portee: This word invites the believer to reflect on the meaning of work. On one hand, Ecclesiastes reminds us that without God's blessing, our toil is in vain. On the other hand, Proverbs affirms that honest work provides for needs and justifies itself. For the Christian, this means that labor is neither absurd nor without value, but must be placed under God's hand and linked to eternal objectives to bear true fruit.

sens: Effort, travail pénible
Souffrance, fatigue physique ou morale
Malheur, affliction
Injustice, iniquité, mal commis intentionnellement
H5999.detail:
1. Pain primarily refers to the effort and labor that is costly. It is the toil one dedicates to living, with its share of fatigue. Ecclesiastes often revisits this reality: "What advantage does man have from all his pain that he takes under the sun?" (Ecclesiastes 1:3). It is useful work, but demanding.
2. Pain can also be the suffering one endures, the pain of the heart or body. Joseph, after his trials, confesses: "God has made me forget all my pains" (Genesis 41:51). Job speaks of his sleepless nights as an incessant pain (Job 7:3).
3. It becomes affliction or broader misfortune: it is the trial that God sends or that circumstances impose. The Psalms often mention this pain as part of the human condition (Psalms 73:5).
4. Finally, pain refers to injustice and intentional wrongdoing, the iniquity committed by one who harms another. One who does harm produces pain: "He who digs a pit will fall into it; he who rolls a stone, it will return upon him" (Proverbs 26:27 is the general idea). The wicked generate pain (Psalms 7:15; Job 4:8).
H5999.origine: The Hebrew word עָמָל (amal) comes from a root that evokes effort, fatigue, and laborious work. Its semantic field oscillates between necessary work and the suffering it entails. The root also appears in verbal forms designating one who works or creates trouble. It is a very common word in biblical wisdom, particularly in Ecclesiastes, where Solomon meditates on the meaning of human work in the face of vanity.
H5999.emploi: The word amal appears 54 times in the Old Testament. It is particularly frequent in the Psalms, Ecclesiastes, and Job, where it expresses the realities of the human condition before God. In Ecclesiastes, it constantly returns to speak of man's work "under the sun" — a work that may seem vain, but is also a divine gift (Ecclesiastes 3:13). In the Psalms, pain appears as the work of the wicked (Psalms 10:7; Psalms 7:15) or as the trial that the righteous endure. Job uses it to express his intense suffering. The word thus carries an ambivalence: it can denote normal and necessary work, the pain suffered, or the injustice perpetrated.
H5999.portee: This word reminds the believer of two biblical realities: first, that work is a legitimate part of human life, a gift from God to live fully, even if it requires effort (Ecclesiastes 3:13). Secondly, that suffering is inherent to our existence — it is not always the result of personal fault, but a dimension of our fleshly condition. This invites the Christian to find in God wisdom and comfort in the face of fatigue and trial, without despairing of present life.
